description.value: The study examined regional BOLD responses and context-dependent functional connectivity during viewing of appetizing versus bland foods, and tested whether individual differences in external food sensitivity modulated these effects.

spans.text: We investigated these issues using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to focus on the neural correlates of viewing appetizing compared with bland foods in healthy volunteers.

value: Our main hypothesis was that the connectivity in the feeding network identified by animal research would be regulated by the interactive effects of viewing appetizing (relative to bland) foods and individual variability in EFS.

value: EFS strongly modulated the change in connectivity between the ventral striatum and amygdala, to the sight of appetizing versus bland foods, and similarly between the ventral striatum and an area of the premotor cortex involved in the preparation of orofacial movements.
A change in connectivity between the ventral striatum and the dorsal ACC was also correlated with EFS.
In both cases, EFS was positively correlated with the change in connectivity ranging from more negative values in low EFS to less negative values in high EFS individuals.

value: For the analysis in which the amygdala was the source region, EFS was negatively correlated with the change in connectivity between the amygdala and both the ventral ACC and the dorsal ACC.
In both cases, the range of the connectivity changes was from more positive values in low EFS to less positive values in high EFS individuals.
We can therefore conclude that in high EFS people there is a reduction in the change in connectivity between specific feeding brain areas when viewing appetizing versus bland food.
